questions.q: If a transversal cuts two parallel lines, how do we describe angles that are on the same side of the transversal and in the same relative position at each intersection?
questions.a: These are called corresponding angles. A wrong answer (like "alternate") suggests the student is mixing up the visual pattern; they likely need to re-draw the intersections and color-code the "top-left" or "bottom-right" positions to see the match.

questions.q: If you have two parallel lines and a transversal, and you know one angle is 60°, how can you determine the measure of its co-interior angle?
questions.a: You subtract 60° from 180° to get 120°. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks all angles created by a transversal are equal; they need to practice distinguishing between equal pairs (corresponding/alternate) and supplementary pairs (co-interior).

questions.q: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle is 110°. What is the measure of its vertically opposite angle, and what is its alternate interior angle?
questions.a: Both are 110°. A wrong answer indicates the student is not yet comfortable with the "equal" property of vertically opposite or alternate angles; they should review the "Z-pattern" for alternate angles.

questions.q: Compare corresponding angles and co-interior angles. Which pair is always equal, and which pair always adds up to 180 degrees?
questions.a: Corresponding angles are always equal, while co-interior angles add up to 180°. A wrong answer shows confusion between the two properties, often caused by trying to memorize definitions instead of visualizing the "opening" of the angles.

questions.q: If a line crosses two lines and the alternate interior angles are NOT equal, what can you conclude about the two lines?
questions.a: The lines are not parallel. A student answering "they are still parallel" is missing the core logic that the properties of angles only hold true when the lines are parallel.

questions.q: Draw a diagram with two parallel lines and a transversal. Label an acute angle as 50°. Can you create a puzzle for a friend using this angle to find all other 7 angles?
questions.a: The student should label the 50° angle and correctly identify that the other angles must be either 50° or 130° (180-50). A poor answer fails to identify the supplementary nature of adjacent angles on a line.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A ______ is a line that intersects two or more other lines at distinct points.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever looked at a railway track with a ______ metal rod crossing over the two parallel rails?

Fill in the blank: Start by identifying angles that look like they are in the "same position" (corresponding) or "opposite sides" (alternate); once you see these patterns, you can use the simple rules—either the angles are equal or they add up to ______ degrees—to solve for any missing value.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify corresponding, alternate, and co-interior angle pairs when a transversal cuts two lines and correctly calculate missing angle measures given that the lines are parallel.
